My point estimates across all three horizons reflect a relatively stable baseline with only modest drift upward over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 297.8 is essentially anchored to the most recent observed price or level, with very little expected movement given typical short-term mean-reversion tendencies and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalysts. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to 298.5 reflects a small positive drift assumption, consistent with a modest bullish bias in the near-term trend while acknowledging that weekly fluctuations tend to average out. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 300.0 represents a round-number convergence point that blends the drift assumption with longer-run fundamental anchoring, essentially suggesting the asset is fairly valued near current levels with gradual appreciation as the base case.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the tight 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 6 points reflects the relatively predictable nature of short-horizon price behavior under normal market conditions, where realized volatility tends to be modest on a daily basis. By one week, the interval widens to approximately plus or minus 12.5 points, capturing the accumulation of daily shocks and the possibility of a macro data release or sentiment shift that could move the needle meaningfully. At one month, the interval expands to plus or minus 25 points, acknowledging that over a four-week window, a wide range of fundamental, technical, and macro forces could realign the price substantially in either direction.

Several specific risks could push outcomes beyond the stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data, a sudden tightening of financial conditions, or a geopolitical shock could produce a sharp selloff that breaks below the lower bound of the one-month interval near 275. Liquidity disruptions or a broader risk-off episode could amplify moves well beyond what historical volatility alone would suggest. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings or economic release, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could propel prices above 325 within a month. These tail risks are real but were assigned low enough probability to sit outside the 90% confidence bands, meaning roughly a 5% chance was assigned to each tail at the monthly horizon.

It is also worth noting that my estimates implicitly assume relatively normal market functioning and no structural breaks.
